title: Bigfoot is not the only mystery worth investigating

content:
Nov 22 2026 - 4:15pm

Little noticed amid the Trump administration’s ongoing release of long-classified files on unidentified flying objects (UFOs), the US National Park Service has released material on another topic of public interest: three files relating to a supposed “Bigfoot” cryptid.

Bigfoot is a supposedly tall, bipedal creature with an ape-human-hybrid-like appearance. Supporters of its existence have pointed to hundreds of eyewitness accounts and footprint casts taken since at least the mid-20th century. These reports have clustered in the US Pacific Northwest.

One of the newly released files involves a newspaper report. Another centers on 1941 testimony from hunters who claimed that an unidentifiable creature carried off an elk they had just shot. But the most interesting report examines footprints apparently left in 1982 by a bipedal creature with extremely large, plainly non-human feet. While an investigator ultimately concluded the tracks were the result of a complex hoax, they added that “if the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail. The ‘print’ marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate.”

To be clear, the lack of DNA evidence and widespread video recordings makes it almost certain that the creature does not exist. Bigfoot has also long been a focus for pranks and hoaxes designed to make money and generate publicity.

Yet the diversity and scale of eyewitness descriptions of apparently extraordinary, unexplained creatures mean that the broader cryptid topic deserves more than scorn. Yes, as with UFOs, most eyewitness reports of cryptids actually result from misidentification and creative imaginations. That said, there are a large number of reports by otherwise credible individuals who claim to have seen very strange things at close proximity in conditions of good visibility. Crucially, these reports predate the modern media age.

Take the Navajo tribal lore surrounding “skinwalkers”, or witches that take the form of strange creatures for malevolent purposes. Former Navajo Rangers Stan Milford and Jonathan Dover conducted extensive investigations into skinwalkers in the early 2000s, coming away convinced that a real phenomenon was involved. Further testimony was collected under a 2010 Department of Defense-contracted study.

That study, which was recently declassified by the Trump administration, records how 25 witnesses, including four police officers and a civil servant, reported having seen cryptids. The report notes that “11 separate individuals witnessed a bipedal ‘dog-like’ creature and/or orbs of light at different times in different locations near the Utah Ranch property.” One theory held by investigators who worked on the report is that the cryptids may be projections or manifestations of an unknown intelligence, perhaps related to UFOs, that are made visible to eyewitnesses for some unknown purpose.

Much caution and healthy skepticism is needed here, of course. For a start, the property referred to in that contracted report is better known as the “Skinwalker Ranch”. The ranch is now the setting for a highly successful, multi-season History Channel television show whose participants claim to conduct scientific research of unexplained phenomena there. Ego and financial gain certainly also motivate their investigations.

Still, a vast array of cryptids have been reported globally for hundreds of years. Given that a small number of truly unexplained UFOs are almost certainly the result of an unknown non-human intelligence of extremely advanced technical capacity, cautious inquiry rather than laughing disdain should be the guiding principle here. Sensationalism is the enemy of good science, but so is reflexive disbelief.

Tom Rogan is a national security writer at the Washington Examiner
